chunks: "Switching frequency is limited by whichever of several things runs out first. The big one is loss.

Every transition has a period where the FET has both voltage and current, so switching loss is about half V times I times the rise-plus-fall time times frequency, and it scales linearly with frequency.
Add the gate-drive power, Q g times V g times f, the output-capacitance loss and the body-diode reverse recovery. All proportional to f.
The heat from those, on top of the conduction loss, sets a thermal ceiling. For a 12 volt, 5 amp example that's about 0.
5 watts at 20 kilohertz but about 2 watts at 500 kilohertz, so with 1. 3 watts of thermal budget the limit is around 250 kilohertz.

Second, speed and timing limits: the gate driver can only deliver so much current, so the edges can only be so fast; dead time of a couple hundred nanoseconds eats 40% of a 1 megahertz period; there's a minimum on-time for the driver and the current-sense blanking, so at high frequency I can't reach low duty cycles; and the bootstrap capacitor needs refresh time.
Third, the controller: a timer has finite resolution, so a 72 megahertz clock with 12-bit duty resolution gives only 17. 6 kilohertz.
Fourth, EMI: faster, more frequent edges mean more harmonics.
And there's a lower limit: too low and the current ripple gets large and the motor whines, below 20 kilohertz it's audible.
So I'd pick something like 20 to 50 kilohertz for a motor, higher for small inductors."
